Use when the user says "deploy X to awsqa", "add Y service to noov-k8s-services", "scaffold a chart", "wire NetBird in the second cluster", or asks about xyops/xySat/xysat-qa, kafka-qa, alloy-qa, headlamp, or the NetBird routing-peer branch.", "tags": [], "related_skills": [], "content": "--- name: noovoleum-k8s-services description: Working with the noovoleum/noov-k8s-services repo — adding/scaffolding services, deploying to awslive or awsqa, navigating the GitOps/ArgoCD/Helm chart conventions, NetBird mesh wiring, and the cluster-topology trap (single-cluster ArgoCD today, no second-cluster path yet). Use when the user says "deploy X to awsqa", "add Y service to noov-k8s-services", "scaffold a chart", "wire NetBird in the second cluster", or asks about xyops/xySat/xysat-qa, kafka-qa, alloy-qa, headlamp, or the NetBird routing-peer branch. version: 1.0 --- # noov-k8s-services — repo conventions and traps ## What this repo is `github.com/noovoleum/noov-k8s-services` is the **GitOps source of truth for the awslive EKS cluster**. ArgoCD runs in awslive and pulls this repo; every `applications/*.yaml` is an ArgoCD `Application` deployed in-cluster. Charts live as siblings of `applications/` (e.g. `xyops/`, `netbird-server/`, `kafka/`). Region: `ap-southeast-1` (Singapore). Accounts: awslive = `656280953066` (prod), awsqa = `307946680298` (QA). **Confirm the deploy model before scaffolding a chart — the repo NAME does not tell you.** `infra-deploy-*` spans both worlds: `infra-deploy-ucoapp-*` is k8s/ArgoCD like this repo, while `infra-deploy-singapore-prod` (+ `-nexus`/`-wellspring`) and `infra-deploy-ucollect-internal-prod` are **Komodo + docker compose stacks, NOT k8s** — no Helm/chart/IngressRoute/PVC/IRSA. One `gh repo clone --depth 5` + `ls` settles it (`stacks/stacks.toml` + `servers/servers.toml` = compose; `applications/*.yaml` = k8s), and it must happen **before any deployment planning**: a whole Supabase-on-EKS design plus a managed-Postgres extension audit was costed against an assumed EKS/RDS target that turned out to be a single EC2 host running compose (2026-08). A Helm chart filed to a compose repo is wrong-repo churn; write a compose stack instead. Full recipe, the world-vs-repo table, and the `ucollect-internal-prod` specifics (single NetBird server, per-stack `cloudflared` ingress, resident Authentik, `/mnt` bind-mounts): `references/komodo-compose-stacks.md`. ## The single biggest trap — single-cluster ArgoCD **Every `applications/*.yaml` uses `destination.server: https://kubernetes.default.svc`.** This is the in-cluster API of whatever cluster ArgoCD itself runs in — currently awslive only. There is **no awsqa destination defined anywhere in the repo today**. No second ArgoCD instance, no cluster-routing scaffolding, no Applications targeting awsqa. Consequences for "deploy X to awsqa" tasks: - You can't just write `applications/xysat-qa.yaml` and have it work — it would deploy to awslive. - Before any awsqa-targeted Application can be added, you need a separate `destination` mechanism. Three options (see references/cluster-topology.md for the decision tree): 1. **Second ArgoCD** in awsqa, with its own `noov-k8s-services` Application and awsqa-side `values-awsqa.yaml` files. 2. **Hub-spoke**: one ArgoCD in awslive, awsqa registered as a managed cluster, new applications use `destination.server: `. 3. **Manual `kubectl apply`** in awsqa (no GitOps for the second cluster). Pick one explicitly with the user. Don't silently default to (1) or (2). ## The QA-has-no-monitoring-stack trap The **QA EKS cluster has no observability stack of its own** — its `monitoring` namespace has been stuck `Terminating` (verified 2026-06), and there is no Prometheus, Grafana, VictoriaMetrics, or Alloy *server* running in QA. QA telemetry is cross-cluster: QA Alloy ships logs/traces/metrics to the **prod** observability plane (`loki.noovoleum.dev`, `tempo.noovoleum.dev`, `vm.noovoleum.dev`). The single Grafana lives in prod `monitoring` and hosts org 1 (provisioned) + org 2 (Noovoleum Dev). Consequence for any "add a QA dashboard / scrape a QA exporter" task: there is **nowhere in QA to scrape or render**. Do NOT try to stand up a QA monitoring stack for this. The proven single-pane pattern is to run the workload (e.g. an AWS-inventory exporter) **in the prod cluster** and have it read the QA account via cross-account `sts:AssumeRole`, so prod Prometheus scrapes it and one Grafana shows both via a `cluster` variable. Full recipe in the `grafana-mcp-observability` skill → `references/aws-inventory-topology-dashboard.md`. ## Two AWS accounts, two SSO sessions, kubectl profile leak - **Use `--use-device-code` for SSO login (user-stated preference, 2026-08).** The default browser-callback flow prints a `127.0.0.1:/oauth/callback` URL that the user pastes back — but the local callback listener dies when the pending authorization expires, so by the time they answer, `curl`ing the callback fails to connect and the whole login has to restart. Device code has no listener to lose: ```bash tmux new-session -d -s ssologin \ "aws sso login --sso-session noov-infra-readonly --use-device-code --no-browser 2>&1 | tee /tmp/sso.log; exec bash" sleep 10; tmux capture-pane -pt ssologin -S -60 | grep -v '^$' | tail -15 ``` Append `; exec bash` so the pane survives the command exiting — otherwise a failed/expired login leaves `no server running` and you can't read what happened. Deliver the `…/start/#/device?user_code=XXXX-XXXX` URL to the user and keep working; poll `aws sts get-caller-identity --profile

` to detect completion. - **Only read-only profiles may exist in `~/.aws/config`.** `infra-readonly-*` is what's configured; there is no admin profile by default. `ReadOnlyAccess` cannot `pods/exec`, snapshot, or apply. To escalate **without a second login** (the same SSO session already grants it — check first): ```bash # list what the session actually grants (token from ~/.aws/sso/cache/*.json) aws sso list-account-roles --region ap-southeast-1 --account-id 656280953066 --access-token "$TOKEN" # → ReadOnlyAccess, GreengrassV2Access, AdministratorAccess ``` Then append a profile reusing the **same `sso_session`** (no re-auth needed): ```ini [profile noov-live-admin] sso_session = noov-infra-readonly sso_account_id = 656280953066 sso_role_name = AdministratorAccess region = ap-southeast-1 ``` `AWS_PROFILE=…` alone does **not** fix kubectl — the kubeconfig `exec` block pins its own profile. Re-run `aws eks update-kubeconfig … --alias noov-prod-admin` and verify with `kubectl --context noov-prod-admin -n auth can-i create pods/exec`. - awslive = `656280953066` (profile `noov-live`), awsqa = `307946680298` (profile `noov-qa`). These are **separate SSO sessions** — `aws sso login --profile noov-live` does NOT auth QA; log in to each separately. Run SSO logins **inside tmux** (user preference) so the device flow survives a dropped foreground; a non-tmux background login can fail with "failed to connect". - **kubectl against QA 401s if prod creds leak into the env.** When you've exported `noov-live` creds (`aws configure export-credentials --format env` / `eval $(...)`) for one task, those `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`/`AWS_SESSION_TOKEN`/`AWS_PROFILE` vars override the QA kubeconfig's `exec` block (which sets `AWS_PROFILE: noov-qa`), so `aws eks get-token` mints a **prod** token against the QA cluster → `the server has asked for the client to provide credentials`. Fix: run QA kubectl with a clean env — `env -u AWS_PROFILE -u AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID -u AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY -u AWS_SESSION_TOKEN kubectl --context noov-qa ...`. - EKS clusters here use `authenticationMode: API` (access entries, not aws-auth ConfigMap). If kubectl 401s even with the right account creds, see the EKS access-entry self-unblock in `grafana-mcp-observability` → `references/grafana-eks-ops-and-multi-org.md`. - **The default `noov-prod` kubeconfig context is READ-ONLY.** It uses `AWS_PROFILE=infra-readonly-live` (a ReadOnlyAccess SSO role), so `kubectl apply`, `helm upgrade`, and `kubectl set resources` all fail with `forbidden: cannot create/patch/delete resource`. For write operations, build a separate context with the admin profile: ```bash AWS_PROFILE=noov-live aws eks update-kubeconfig --region ap-southeast-1 \ --name noovoleum-prod-eks-cluster --alias noov-prod-admin # pin the profile into the context's exec env so it doesn't fall back to read-only: kubectl config set-credentials --exec-env AWS_PROFILE=noov-live ``` Use `kubectl --context noov-prod-admin` for all writes. Same pattern for QA: `AWS_PROFILE=noov-qa ... --alias noov-qa-admin`. Verify with `kubectl --context noov-prod-admin auth can-i create deployments -n monitoring` → `yes`. ## The NetBird mesh trap — the 2026-06-08 incident The `netbird-server/` umbrella chart in this repo bundles a **client DaemonSet** (toggled `client.enabled: true`) that runs `hostNetwork: true` + privileged (`NET_ADMIN`, `NET_RAW`) on every node. There is a **documented production incident on 2026-06-08** where this DaemonSet shadowed AWS VPC CNI ip rules (prio 105/110 vs CNI prio 1536) and corrupted cross-node pod-to-pod routing cluster-wide — Kafka timeouts, MongoDB DNS failures, control-plane CrashLoops. The post-mortem lives in `docs/post-mortem-netbird-eni.md` on the routing-peer branch. **Replacement design on `feat/netbird-routing-peer` (PR #15, open):** a single non-hostNetwork `routing-peer` Deployment, HA 2 replicas with pod-anti-affinity, the setup key in OpenBao via ExternalSecret, network routes + nameserver groups configured in the NetBird dashboard. The old DaemonSet is left in the chart with `client.enabled: false` and a comment "deprecated, must not be re-enabled." **Rule of thumb for any new NetBird client wiring (including awsqa):** adopt `feat/netbird-routing-peer` first. Do not deploy a per-node client DaemonSet on a fresh cluster without reading the post-mortem. References/cluster-topology.md has the full NetBird decision matrix. ## Chart conventions ### Standalone vs umbrella - **Umbrella charts** wrap upstream Helm deps via `Chart.yaml` `dependencies:` (e.g. `netbird-server/`, `loki/`, `traefik-private/`, `grafana/`). - **Standalone charts** write their own templates in `templates/` (e.g. `xyops/`, `cronicle/`, `kafka/`, `headlamp/`). ### Umbrella charts with NO Chart.yaml in the repo (prometheus/ — grafana/ is FIXED) > ⚠️ **STALE for `grafana/` as of 2026-08 — re-verified on a fresh clone.** `grafana/` > now HAS a real `Chart.yaml` (umbrella `version: 1.1.0`, `appVersion: "12.3.1"`, > dependency `grafana/grafana 10.5.15`) plus `templates/`, `dashboards/`, `alerting/`, > and `values-secret.example.yaml`. `helm dependency build grafana/` then > `helm template grafana ./grafana -f grafana/values.yaml` works directly — **no umbrella > reconstruction needed**. Budget ~2 min for `helm dependency build`; it exceeds a 60s > command timeout, so pass `timeout=180`+. The recipe below still applies to > `prometheus/`. Always `ls` the chart dir before assuming which case you're in. Both `grafana/` and `prometheus/` ship as **values.yaml-only** directories — no `Chart.yaml` or `charts/` subdirectory in the repo. The live Helm release wraps an upstream subchart (`grafana/grafana:10.5.15` and `kube-prometheus-stack:82.8.0` respectively) but the Chart.yaml is generated on-the-fly during deploy. **To helm-upgrade these charts with new values, you must reconstruct the umbrella locally:** 1. Create a `Chart.yaml` with the subchart dependency: ```yaml apiVersion: v2 name: version: 1.0.0 dependencies: - name: version: repository: ``` 2. `helm repo add && helm dependency build .` 3. **Extract custom templates from the live release** — these umbrellas have custom templates (IngressRoute, ServiceMonitor, etc.) that are NOT in the upstream subchart. If you deploy the bare subchart without them, the external route disappears and the site 404s. Extract with: ```bash helm --kube-context -n get manifest | \ awk '/# Source: \/templates\/.yaml/{p=1} p{print} /^---/{if(p){p=0}}' \ > templates/.yaml # then clean '# Source:' and '---' lines with sed ``` 4. `.gitignore` the generated `charts/` and `Chart.lock` (build artifacts). 5. `helm upgrade . -n -f values.yaml` (uses the local umbrella). **Critical:** verify your rendered output preserves custom templates before applying — `helm template ... | grep 'Source: /templates/'` should show the custom template names. See `grafana-mcp-observability` → `references/mongodb-atlas-prometheus-integration.md` for the full Prometheus-umbrella reconstruction worked example. ### Three patterns for prod vs QA The repo uses **all three** patterns. Don't assume one: 1. **Sibling chart** — `kafka/` + `kafka-qa/`, `alloy/` + `alloy-qa/` (per CLAUDE.md directory tree, but see pitfall below). Two completely separate chart directories, two separate ArgoCD Applications. 2. **In-chart QA templates** — `headlamp/templates/*-qa.yaml` gated by `qa.applyToQACluster` flag. Single chart, conditional rendering. 3. **Values-file QA** — `redpanda/values-prod.yaml` + `redpanda/values-qa.yaml`. Same chart, different `helm -f` files. ### Pitfall: stale CLAUDE.md references The directory tree in `CLAUDE.md` lists `kafka-qa/` and `alloy-qa/` as sibling charts. **`alloy-qa/` does not exist on disk** at HEAD of `main` or `feat/netbird-routing-peer` (verified by `git ls-tree`). It's either planned, removed, or lives in a private branch. Do not assume "the alloy-qa pattern" works as described in CLAUDE.md — verify on disk first. `kafka-qa/` may or may not exist; check `git ls-tree -r HEAD --name-only | grep kafka` before modeling on it. ### Traefik IngressRoute convention (private vs public) For `traefik.io/v1alpha1` `IngressRoute` resources in this repo, do **not** add `spec.ingressClassName` (that's for standard `Ingress`, not the Traefik CRD pattern). Use `metadata.annotations.kubernetes.io/ingress.class: traefik` (public) or `traefik-private` (private) + `external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/target: `. See `noovoleum-infra-traefik-routing` skill for the full IngressRoute reference. ### Helm hardening defaults inherited from the xyops PR The live `xyops/` chart (PR #14, merged 2026-06-11) introduced a hardening pattern that the post-merge follow-ups (#16–19) preserved: - `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` - `runAsNonRoot: true` + `runAsUser: 65532` - `capabilities.drop: [ALL]` - Writable `emptyDir` mounts for runtime paths (logs, run, tmp) - `seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault` - `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: ServerSideApply=true` on the Application Follow-ups #16–19 (all merged 2026-06-11) addressed ArgoCD drift on: - StatefulSet server-default fields (`fix/xyops-argocd-sts-drift`) - kube-defaulted fields under SSA (`fix/xyops-ssa-defaults`) - VolumeClaimTemplates apiVersion/kind drift (`fix/xyops-vct-apiversion`) - Permanent OutOfSync, fixed with ServerSideDiff (`fix/xyops-serversidediff`) When adding a new chart that uses StatefulSet + PVCs + SSA, **copy the `ignoreDifferences` block from `applications/xyops.yaml` verbatim** — those patterns are known to drift and the existing PRs already document the fix. ### Stateless service chart pattern (no PVC → Deployment, no SSA drift machinery) Not every new service needs a StatefulSet + PVCs + the full `ignoreDifferences`/`ServerSideDiff` apparatus. A **stateless** service (sidecar API, MCP server, exporter proxy, anything with no local state) uses the lighter shape: `Deployment` + `Service` + `IngressRoute` + (if it needs a secret) `ExternalSecret`, gated `namespace.yaml` with `create: false` when the namespace already exists. No `volumeClaimTemplates`, so **none of the xyops SSA-drift machinery applies** — the Application can be the minimal shape (sync-wave, `ServerSideApply=true`, no `ignoreDifferences`, no `ServerSideDiff`). Worked example: `grafana-mcp/` (PR #32) — see `references/stateless-chart-pattern.md`. ### Single-PVC + S3 blobs + IRSA (the middle case, neither pole) A third shape the two references above don't cover: an app whose **bulk data lives in S3** but that keeps **one small durable local file** (SQLite DB, cache index). Do **not** reach for a StatefulSet — use a `Deployment` + a **standalone `PersistentVolumeClaim`** (RWO, single replica, `strategy: Recreate` so the RWO volume isn't double-mounted mid-rollout). A plain PVC object doesn't drift like `volumeClaimTemplates`, so the whole xyops SSA-drift chain is skipped. S3 access is via a **ServiceAccount annotated with an IAM role (IRSA)** — SDKs auto-pick the web-identity token, never static keys; bucket + role are created out-of-band, the chart carries only the annotation slot. Mirror the S3-vs-local choice with an app-level `STORAGE_BACKEND` env so local dev needs no AWS; ExternalSecret still handles the app's own non-AWS secrets (session key, OIDC secret). Worked example: `bbox-labeler/` — full recipe (PVC template, IRSA SA, `Recreate`, storage seam, backend-flip validation) in `references/pvc-plus-s3-chart-pattern.md`. ### Provisioning sidecar dashboards into a specific org (`provider.orgid`) The Grafana chart's `grafana-sc-dashboard` sidecar discovers k8s/infra dashboard ConfigMaps (labeled `grafana_dashboard=1`, emitted by kube-prometheus-stack via `forceDeployDashboards: true`) and imports them. **Which org they land in is controlled by `grafana.sidecar.dashboards.provider.orgid`** (upstream default `1`), NOT by the ConfigMap or by `forceDeployDashboards`. The ConfigMap label controls *whether* the sidecar imports a dashboard; `forceDeployDashboards` controls *whether KPS emits the ConfigMaps at all*; neither scopes to an org. To auto-provision the k8s dashboards into **org 2** (Noovoleum Dev) instead of org 1, set in `grafana/values.yaml`: ```yaml grafana: sidecar: dashboards: enabled: true label: grafana_dashboard labelValue: "1" searchNamespace: monitoring provider: name: sidecarProvider orgid: 2 # ← the lever (default 1) folder: 'Kubernetes' type: file ``` Keep `prometheus/values.yaml` → `kube-prometheus-stack.grafana.forceDeployDashboards: true` so the ConfigMaps still flow. Verified live (2026-07): all 18 `provisioned: true` dashboards in org 1 are k8s/infra stock (apiserver, k8s-resources-*, kubelet, coredns, prometheus/grafana-overview) — **zero app dashboards are sidecar-backed** (the custom ucoBox/ClickHouse/etc. dashboards are all `provisioned: false`, API-created) — so retargeting the provider moves exactly the infra set. **PITFALL — the wrong lever (PR #33, closed/superseded):** setting `forceDeployDashboards: false` does NOT retarget to org 2 — it stops KPS from emitting the ConfigMaps entirely, killing auto-provisioning rather than retargeting it. Use `provider.orgid` for org retargeting; reserve `forceDeployDashboards: false` for when you want the dashboards gone from *every* org and re-imported manually via API. The general "Grafana has no cross-org move API; provisioned dashboards can't be deleted via API either" constraint is in the `grafana-mcp-observability` skill → "Cross-org dashboard movement". **Deploy caveat:** `grafana/values.yaml` in this repo targets the `grafana.noovoleum.dev` private instance. If the prod `grafana.noovoleum.site` Grafana is deployed from a different chart (it is — see ".site is prod" below), the same `provider.orgid: 2` change must be mirrored there for prod to see it. ### Values-only-chart release-name trap (Grafana, Prometheus) `grafana/` and `prometheus/` are values-only dirs in this repo (no `Chart.yaml` — see "Umbrella charts with NO Chart.yaml" above). A consequence that bites any *new* in-cluster client of those services: **the Helm release name is not visible from Git**, so the in-cluster Service DNS (`-grafana.monitoring.svc.cluster.local`) can't be read from the repo. When wiring a new client (e.g. `GRAFANA_URL` for grafana-mcp, a scrape target for an exporter), either (a) verify the Service name against the live release first — `kubectl -n monitoring get svc -l app.kubernetes.io/name=grafana` — or (b) fall back to the public Traefik URL, which always works and needs no release-name guess. Don't hard-code an assumed release name without one of these checks. ### Grafana: `grafana/` in this repo IS prod `.site` (corrected 2026-08) > ⚠️ **The section below is STALE — re-verified on a fresh clone 2026-08.** The > `grafana/` chart in this repo is now the **PROD** `grafana.noovoleum.site` > deployment, fully GitOps-managed. Do NOT repeat the old advice that "prod's > chart is not in this repo" — it costs a wrong-path detour at the start of any > Grafana task. Verified on `main`: > - `grafana/Chart.yaml` — real umbrella (`version: 1.1.0`, `appVersion "12.3.1"`, > dependency `grafana/grafana 10.5.15`) > - `grafana/values.yaml` — `ingressRoute.host: grafana.noovoleum.site`, **public** > `kubernetes.io/ingress.class: traefik`, NLB `a64d1600…` > - `applications/grafana.yaml` — ArgoCD Application, `path: grafana`, > `targetRevision: main`, `automated: {prune: true, selfHeal: true}`, > `ServerSideApply=true` + `ServerSideDiff=true` > - Secrets via ESO → `openbao-infra` ClusterSecretStore, `remotePath: grafana` > (→ `infra/grafana`), Secret `grafana-secret` > > **Consequence: never `helm upgrade` prod Grafana by hand.** The change is a PR > to `grafana/values.yaml`; ArgoCD syncs it. And because `selfHeal: true` + > `prune: true` are on, **any manual `kubectl`/`helm` change is reverted within > seconds** — including a `kubectl scale` to 0 for maintenance. A real rollback > must go through Git, or first suspend automation — see the app-of-apps trap > below for the procedure that actually works. > Factor that into the rollback plan for **any** stateful prod app in this repo, > not just Grafana. ### PITFALL: suspending automated sync — merge-null fails, and the PARENT re-arms it Verified the hard way during the Grafana 13 upgrade (2026-08). Two traps stack: 1. **`--type merge` with `automated: null` silently does nothing.** This widely-copied command reports `application.argoproj.io/grafana patched` and leaves `automated: {prune: true, selfHeal: true}` intact: ```bash # ✗ DOES NOT WORK — reports success, changes nothing kubectl -n argocd patch application grafana --type merge \ -p '{"spec":{"syncPolicy":{"automated":null}}}' ``` Use a JSON-patch `remove` instead: ```bash kubectl -n argocd patch application --type json \ -p '[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/syncPolicy/automated"}]' ``` 2. **Every child Application here is itself managed by the `noov-k8s-services` app-of-apps**, so patching only the child gets reverted within seconds — the parent re-applies the child's spec from Git. Check for `argocd.argoproj.io/tracking-id: noov-k8s-services:argoproj.io/Application:argocd/` in the child's annotations; if present, suspend **parent first, then child**: ```bash A="kubectl -n argocd" $A patch application noov-k8s-services --type json -p '[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/syncPolicy/automated"}]' $A patch application --type json -p '[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/syncPolicy/automated"}]' # ALWAYS verify it actually stuck — the patch reporting success is not proof: $A get application -o jsonpath='{.spec.syncPolicy.automated}{"\n"}' # must be empty ``` Restore in reverse (child, then parent) with a merge patch re-adding `{"automated":{"prune":true,"selfHeal":true}}`, then confirm both report `Synced/Healthy` and that ArgoCD did not revert your work. **Symptom that means you hit this:** `kubectl scale deploy X --replicas=0` appears to work, then `spec.replicas` is back to 1 with a *new* pod, and `kubectl get events` shows `ScalingReplicaSet ... from 0 to 1` seconds later. Don't fight it by re-scaling in a loop — fix the sync policy. The `grafana/values.yaml` in this repo targets `grafana.noovoleum.**dev**` / `traefik-private` / NLB `a016f631…`. **That is NOT the Grafana most users/clients mean.** Verified empirically (2026-07, `curl /api/health`): - `grafana.noovoleum.**site**` → **200** — the **PROD** Grafana (org 1 + org 2), public traefik, internet-facing NLB `a64d1600…`. Its chart is **NOT in this repo** (deployed separately). - `grafana.noovoleum.**dev**` → **times out publicly** — a private `traefik-private` instance, only reachable in-cluster/mesh. Consequences for a new chart that talks to "the Grafana": - `GRAFANA_URL` for a prod-facing client = `https://grafana.noovoleum.site` (public URL is verified-correct since prod's chart isn't in Git and its in-cluster Service name is unknowable from here). - An IngressRoute for a prod-facing service uses **public** `traefik` class + NLB `a64d1600…`, not `traefik-private` / `a016f631…`. - A `/mcp`-style path on `grafana.noovoleum.site` co-exists with Grafana's bare `Host()` IngressRoute via Traefik Host+PathPrefix specificity — **but** verify Grafana's route has no forward-auth/SSO middleware that would inherit onto the new path (would bounce non-browser clients). If it does, mint a dedicated hostname instead. Full worked example + the `.site`/`.dev` table: `references/stateless-chart-pattern.md`. # Linux Host Resource Pressure

Use when a Linux service is failing or stalling and the host may be short on disk, memory, swap, PIDs, file descriptors, or I/O capacity. Fix the constrained layer; do not restart the service until active work is understood.

## Diagnose first

Capture fresh evidence in parallel:

```bash
df -h / /home; df -ih / /home
free -h; swapon --show
cat /proc/pressure/{cpu,memory,io}
ps -eLf --no-headers | wc -l
cat /proc/sys/kernel/{pid_max,threads-max}
```

For a systemd service, inspect both unit and parent slice:

```bash
systemctl show SERVICE -p MainPID -p TasksCurrent -p TasksMax -p MemoryCurrent -p MemoryPeak -p MemoryHigh -p MemoryMax
CG=$(systemctl show SERVICE -p ControlGroup --value)
for f in pids.current pids.max pids.events memory.current memory.high memory.max memory.swap.current memory.events; do
  test -r "/sys/fs/cgroup$CG/$f" && { printf '%s=' "$f"; cat "/sys/fs/cgroup$CG/$f"; }
done
systemctl status SERVICE --no-pager   # inspect the whole cgroup process tree
ps -eo pid,ppid,rss,stat,etime,args --sort=-rss | head -30
```

A healthy host can still have a starved service. If `free` shows headroom but the service sits at `MemoryHigh`, inspect its descendants: shells, tmux servers, builds, tests, and agent jobs may have inherited the control-plane cgroup. Temporarily raising the service's runtime high-water mark can preserve active work and confirm throttling, but the durable fix is a sibling workload slice/transient service. Supervisors should retain control handles, not arbitrary workloads, in their own cgroup.

Interpret `EAGAIN`/`Errno 11` from evidence, not the message alone:

- PID/thread exhaustion: `pids.events max`, `TasksCurrent≈TasksMax`, or `RLIMIT_NPROC`.
- Memory throttling: high/full memory PSI plus rising `memory.events: high` or `sock_throttled`; this can make IPC and worker startup fail transiently without an OOM kill.
- Nonblocking IPC/file locks: reproduce through the lowest-level local protocol and retain the exception type; wrappers often discard it.
- Disk/I/O pressure: low free blocks/inodes or high full I/O PSI.

## Disk cleanup

1. Measure before deleting.
2. Check live command lines, environments, cwd/exe links, and open file descriptors before touching build targets, temp directories, or sockets. Match an exact path boundary (`candidate == target || candidate starts with target + "/"`): substring/prefix checks falsely report `/target-dev` as a reference to `/target`. Exclude the scanner process and its invoking ancestor shell, whose own argv contains the target solely because it is running the proof.
3. Prefer bounded platform cleanup: journal vacuum/cap, package-manager cache, then inactive reproducible build caches.
4. Preserve active build targets even if they are the largest directories.
5. Re-measure disk and verify critical services afterward.

A shared build target prevents per-worktree duplication but is not self-bounding. Measure its `debug/`, `release/`, incremental, and dependency trees separately. After verification, an inactive shared `debug/` tree can be reclaimed while preserving pinned release deployment artifacts—but only after proving no live process references that exact target path. Also expire inactive runner/workspace caches; “cache” is not permanent storage.

Prevent recurrence at the owning layer, e.g. a journald drop-in with bounded `SystemMaxUse`, `RuntimeMaxUse`, and retention, plus disk preflight and cache-retention policy for broad builds.

### Multi-GB `~/.hermes/state.db` is usually the search index, not conversations

Before pruning history, measure WHERE the bytes are. `dbstat` gives per-object
page usage (sqlite3 CLI has it; the `sqlite3` Python module on the same host may
too — try it before assuming):

```bash
python3 -c "
import sqlite3;c=sqlite3.connect('file:$HOME/.hermes/state.db?mode=ro',uri=True)
for n,m,p in c.execute('select name, sum(pgsize)/1048576.0, count(*) from dbstat group by name order by 2 desc limit 12'):
    print(f'{m:9.1f} MB  {n}')"
```

Typical heavy-user finding: `messages` (the real data) is a fraction of total,
while `messages_fts_trigram_data` + `*_fts_content` + `*_fts_trigram_content`
dominate. That is the **legacy pre-v23 FTS layout**, which keeps a full
duplicate copy of every message *twice* and trigram-indexes tool output. Since
`tool`-role rows are usually ~90% of content bytes, most of the file is index
for terminal spew.

Fix is first-party, resumable, throttled, and touches no conversation data:

```bash
hermes sessions optimize-storage --yes     # rebuild in v23 external-content layout + VACUUM
```

Preflight: it needs free disk ≈ current DB size (it says so and prompts).
Snapshot first — `sqlite3 state.db ".backup 'state.db.bak-$(date +%F-%H%M%S)'"`,
which is WAL-safe against the live gateway (~2 min for 3.6 GB).

Measured on Terminus 2026-08-13 (2,922 sessions / 242,664 messages):
**3475.9 MB → 1460.5 MB, 2015 MB reclaimed (58%)**, ~20 min foreground.
`*_fts_content` and `*_fts_trigram_content` (607 MB each) disappear entirely;
`messages` is untouched. Verify after with `pragma quick_check`, session/message
counts, and `select count(*) from messages_fts` matching the `messages` count —
the rebuild is only trustworthy if the index row count still equals the table's.

- Check `pragma freelist_count` before reaching for a bare `VACUUM`: a low
  freelist means VACUUM reclaims nothing and the index rebuild is the only lever.
- Do NOT reach for `hermes sessions prune` first. Pruning deletes real history
  to reclaim part of the *small* half. Rebuild the index, re-measure, and only
  then decide if age-based pruning is still worth it.
- `messages` has no `created_at` column — age-bucket by `sessions.started_at`
  (a REAL unix epoch, so `strftime('%Y-%m', started_at, 'unixepoch')`).

## Don't fill a shared host: preflight before installs and builds

A dependency install or image build on a box that also runs live services can
drive `/` to 100% and take those services down. Observed 2026-08-13 on a shared
build host: a `pnpm install` (~4,800 packages) for a *cosmetic* i18n string fix
filled the disk; Postgres, Kong and Realtime in a running Docker Swarm stack all
dropped to `0/1`.

**Preflight — cost the operation against real headroom, not total capacity:**

```bash
df -h /                     # free space NOW
docker system df            # RECLAIMABLE column = your actual budget
```

Rough footprints worth respecting: a JS monorepo `node_modules` 2–4 GB, a
multi-stage app image 2.5 GB per app, a Rust `target/` 5–15 GB. If free space is
under ~2× the expected footprint on a host with live services, **do the work
elsewhere or skip it**. A cosmetic fix never justifies risking a running stack.

**Reclaim order on a shared host — cheapest and least destructive first:**

```bash
docker builder prune -af                      # build cache, zero risk
docker image prune -af --filter "until=1h"    # keeps recently-tagged images
docker image prune -f                         # dangling only
```

**Untagged layers are only half of it — look for *tagged but unused* images.**
`docker system df -v` shows a `CONTAINERS` count per image; any tagged image at
`0` is a stopped side project holding whole gigabytes that no prune filter will
touch. Measured 2026-08-14: dangling prune freed 2.28 GB, then removing four
tagged-but-unused images (`mongo:7`, `postgres:16`, `redis:7`, `node:22`) took a
93%-full disk to 86% — **6 GB total, all re-pullable**:

```bash
docker system df -v | sed -n '/^Images space/,/^Containers space/p'  # read CONTAINERS col
docker rmi mongo:7 postgres:16 redis:7 node:22
sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=200M && sudo apt-get clean
```

Do this *before* deleting a teammate's build cache: it is larger, faster, and
recovers with one `docker pull`.

**Never `rm -rf` a root-owned tree with stderr attached to a tool call.** A
container-created pnpm store, removed as the unprivileged user, emitted
**29 million characters** of `Permission denied` — one line per file — flooding
the transcript. Redirect and re-run with privilege:

```bash
sudo rm -rf /path/to/tree >/dev/null 2>&1; echo "rc=$?"
```

Docker is usually the largest single consumer (`/var/lib/docker` was 34 GB of a
90 GB disk here) and is almost entirely regenerable. Prefer it over deleting
another team's build caches — and if you must touch those, check for live
builders first (`ps aux | grep -E 'cargo-watch|rustc'`) and leave the watched
target alone.

**On a host you don't own, report the breakdown and ask before the second
round.** Regenerable Docker artifacts are yours to prune unilaterally. Another
team's build caches and a user's toolchains are not — measured 2026-08-14, the
top consumers on a shared box were `.gradle` 7.9 GB, `android-sdk` 7.4 GB,
`.bun` 3.3 GB, `.android` 3.3 GB, `flutter` 2.3 GB: all trivially deletable, all
someone's working environment, and none of it mine to decide. Produce the table,
name what is safe (dangling layers, unused tagged images, journal, apt cache)
with its total, and let the owner pick:

```bash
sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 / 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -8
sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 /home/<user> 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -20
```

Deleting a shared build cache to unblock your own task, then discovering it was
mid-build, is a self-inflicted outage on someone else's work. Asking costs one
message.

**`rm -rf` on a huge tree is not instant.** Deleting a `node_modules` with
hundreds of thousands of inodes ran for **20+ minutes** under load average ~8
and still showed 2.4 GB remaining. Don't block on it and don't assume it failed:
run it detached and poll.

```bash
nohup rm -rf /path/to/node_modules >/dev/null 2>&1 &
pgrep -f 'rm -rf' >/dev/null && echo "still running" || echo "done"
```

Reclaim space from a *different* source in parallel rather than waiting.

**Recovery is usually automatic — verify, don't rebuild.** Swarm/Kubernetes
reschedule failed tasks once space returns; all 14 services returned to `1/1`
with no manual intervention. Prove data survived before declaring recovery:

```bash
docker exec "$PG" psql -U postgres -tAc \
  "select count(*) from information_schema.tables where table_schema='public';"
```

Matching the pre-incident count (461 here) is the evidence. Tearing down and
re-migrating on the assumption of corruption would have destroyed a good DB.

## Zram trial

Use zram when disk swap is active and memory/I/O PSI shows swap stalls. Zram trades CPU and some RAM for compressed swap; it does not fix a memory leak.

Default conservative trial for a small, CPU-constrained host:

- zram logical size: about 25% of RAM (often 2 GiB on an 8 GiB host)
- compression: `lz4`
- priority: `100`
- keep disk swap at lower priority as fallback

Prefer the distro's `systemd-zram-generator` over a custom unit. See [references/zram-systemd-generator.md](references/zram-systemd-generator.md) for the known-good setup, activation pitfall, verification, rollback, and reassessment checklist.

## Post-reboot forensics: crash, OOM, or commanded shutdown?

After an unexpected reboot, distinguish the three before blaming anything.
All evidence is in the previous boot's journal and the sysstat archive:

```bash
# 1. How did the previous boot END? A graceful poweroff leaves a trail; a crash doesn't.
sudo journalctl -b -1 --no-pager | tail -50
# graceful:  "guest-shutdown called" / "Reached target poweroff.target" / systemd-shutdown syncing
# crash:     journal just stops mid-activity, no shutdown target lines

# 2. Who commanded it? auditd catches the execve:
sudo ausearch -ts <HH:MM> -te <HH:MM> -m EXECVE | grep -B2 -A2 poweroff
# e.g. ppid=<qemu-ga pid> + a0="/sbin/poweroff" = the hypervisor/user requested it

# 3. Was there an OOM before it? (journalctl -k of previous boot)
sudo journalctl -b -1 -k --no-pager | grep -iE 'out of memory|oom-kill'

# 4. What was the load/memory in the minutes before? sysstat has it even if the
#    journal is noisy — sa files survive the reboot:
sar -q ALL -f /var/log/sysstat/sa$(date +%d) -s 09:45:00 -e 10:18:00   # runq, ldavg, PSI
sar -r ALL -f /var/log/sysstat/sa$(date +%d) -s 09:45:00 -e 10:18:00   # memory
```

`sar -q ALL` includes the `%scpu/%sio/%smem` PSI columns — a pre-reboot sample
showing ldavg-1=196 with 99% some-I/O PSI and 92% some-memory PSI is the
smoking gun for saturation-then-forced-poweroff, and zero OOM lines rules out
kernel intervention. Report the mechanism (who ran poweroff) separately from
the trigger (what saturated the host): the user force-restarting because the
the box hung is both — the qemu-ga poweroff is theirs, the saturation is the bug.

Full worked example (kanban agent fan-out → PSI saturation → forced poweroff)
plus the two-layer containment pattern (cgroup ceiling on the parent service +
application concurrency caps): [references/host-crash-forensics.md](references/host-crash-forensics.md).

## Catching an external SIGKILL sender

When a process dies with `code=killed, status=9/KILL` and it's NOT OOM
(memory modest, `OOMKills=0`, no memory pressure), something external is
sending `kill -9`. The journal only shows the death, not the killer. Use the
Linux audit subsystem to catch the sender:

```bash
# Add audit rule for SIGKILL (signal 9 = 0x9):
sudo auditctl -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S kill -F a1=0x9 -F key=sigkill_sender
# For tgkill, the signal is in a2, not a1:
sudo auditctl -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S tgkill -F a2=0x9 -F key=sigkill_sender

# After the next kill, pull the trail:
sudo ausearch -k sigkill_sender -ts recent
```

The `proctitle` field is hex-encoded — decode it to see the exact kill command:

```bash
python3 -c "print(bytes.fromhex('<hex>').decode('ascii', errors='replace'))"
```

Common finding: the app kills itself. Apps with a "kill all existing instances
on startup" pattern (via `ps aux` + pattern match + `kill -9`) mutual-kill
under systemd `Restart=on-failure`. Fix: stop/disable the service, or remove
the self-killing startup code. See
[references/sigkill-sender-audit.md](references/sigkill-sender-audit.md) for
a full worked example (9router mutual kill loop).

## Verification

A fix is incomplete until all applicable checks pass:

- constrained resource has measurable headroom;
- service health endpoint or native status succeeds;
- active workloads were not killed;
- kernel/cgroup counters stop worsening under representative load;
- persistence is verified (`generated`/enabled unit plus readable config);
- package manager is clean after an interrupted transaction (`dpkg --audit` on Debian-family systems).

## Pitfalls

- Do not infer PID exhaustion from `Errno 11`; memory-backed socket throttling can produce the same user-visible symptom.
- When serializing Cargo work with `flock`, use `flock -o LOCKFILE cargo …` (`--close`). Without it, rustc may start a persistent `sccache` server that inherits the lock file descriptor and holds the lock after Cargo exits, deadlocking every later build. Diagnose with `fuser -v LOCKFILE`; terminate stale waiters and stop the sccache server before retrying.
- Do not delete a large Cargo/Node target while its command line references that target.
- Do not force existing disk-swapped pages into new zram under load; new swap will prefer the higher priority naturally.
- A package post-install may activate zram with defaults before local config exists. Verify the live size and selected algorithm, not just the generated swap priority.
